nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life on land|Desertification mitigation|Vegetation cover expansion_qna_000
nodes.label: Taxonomy
nodes.question: What types of vegetation are found in the region surrounding Xalapa?
nodes.answer: The surrounding vegetation types include cloud forest to pine-oak forest, tropical montane cloud forests, tropical dry forests, and riparian vegetation.
nodes.paragraph: Materials and methods Study area We conducted this study in Xalapa, Veracruz, Mexico (19 32 49 N, 96 54 41 W), a conurbation with a popula - tion of ~ 550,0 inhabitants and an extension of ~ 59.54 km2 (Falf n et al. 2018 ; INEGI 2021 ). Xalapa is located on the eastern slope of the Trans-Mexican V olcanic Belt (eleva - tion range: 1120 1720 masl; INEGI 2010 ), in the transition zone where the Nearctic and Neotropic biogeographical regions converge and their biotas overlap (Morrone 2015 ). Additionally, the city is surrounded by contrasting vegeta - tion types influenced by the two main clime regimes of the region: temperate humid and semi-warm humid (Lemoine- Rodr guez et al. 2019 ). The original vegetation types cover - ing the region where the city is now located consisted of: (1) a transition zone from cloud forest to pine-oak forest to the North; (2) tropical montane cloud forests in the cen - tral Southwestern section; (3) tropical dry forests in the central Southeast, and (4) riparian vegetation along the multiple streams that run through the city (Castillo-Cam - pos 1991 ).

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life on land|Desertification mitigation|Vegetation cover expansion_qna_001
nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What percentage of Xalapa's territory is covered by vegetation?
nodes.answer: Nearly 40% of Xalapa's territory is covered by vegetation.
nodes.paragraph: Despite its continuously growing urban matrix (Lemoine-Rodr guez et al. 2019), Xalapa is considered to have a high vegetation cover, with nearly ~ 40% of its ter - ritory covered by vegetation (Falf n et al. 2018 ), mainly distributed across its greenspace network, both comprised by public (i.e., parks, median strips, reserves) and private property (i.e., gardens, forest patches). Woody vegetation in Xalapa is diverse and heterogeneous, with the configuration of the trees and shrubs mainly shaped by the necessities and preferences of citizens and government plans (Falf in and MacGregor-Fors 2016 ). Survey design We followed a citywide survey scheme (Turner 2003 ; Mac - Gregor-Fors 2019 ) to gather a representative sample of the bird communities in the urban continuum of Xalapa. For this city, a sampling design was established in 2013 and has been continuously utilized for different biodiversity surveys (e.g., Ram rez-Restrepo et al. 2015 ; Escobar-lb ez and MacGregor-Fors 2016 ; Falf n and MacGregor-Fors 2016 ). nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life on land|Desertification mitigation|Vegetation cover expansion_qna_002
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What size were the subplots used for estimating bryophyte cover?
nodes.answer: The subplots used for estimating bryophyte cover were 0.5 m² in size.
nodes.paragraph: The weeding took place three times a year in April, July, and September. Having these two subsections on each plot enabled us to separate the effects of weeding on bryophyte cover and richness from the other treatment effects. The whole field was mown twice per year in mid-June and mid-August to simulate intermediate grassland management. Cut biomass was removed after mowing. For more information on the experimental setup see Pichon et al. 36. Vegetation sampling From March to April 2023, we conducted a vegetation survey of the bryophyte species (all bryophytes were collected before the annual fertilization). We sampled all bryophyte species and visually estimated their cover in both the unweeded subplot and a part of the weeded subplot of the same size (0.5 m m . We collected bryophyte species that we were unable to identify in the field for later identification in the lab. The nomenclature of bryophytes follows Hodgetts et al. 2020 52. For the subsequent analyses, we summed up the cover estimates of each species and species counts for total bryophyte cover and species richness values per subplot.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life on land|Desertification mitigation|Vegetation cover expansion_qna_003
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What was excluded from the initial models and why?
nodes.answer: Winter cover of vascular plants was excluded from the initial models because it was never significant.
nodes.paragraph: Additionally, we visually estimated the percentage cover of vascular plants in a summer campaign in August 2022 and a winter campaign in March/April 2023. We measured the summer cover of vascular plants because shading from vascular plants is likely to be most important when vascular plant biomass is high. Vascular plant winter cover may also be important as some bryophyte species (especially those from arable land) are short- lived and develop mostly from late summer on 53 and then grow throughout winter as long as temperatures remain above freezing. Open gaps in the vegetation cover can then be colonized. We therefore included both summer and winter cover of vascular plants in our initial models but finally excluded winter cover as it was never significant. In the unweeded subplots, the species richness of vascular plants had changed substantially over time and we therefore estimated the realized richness of these subplots in August 2022. To calculate the functional composition of the vascular plant community, we measured the specific leaf area (SLA) of the 20 sown target species in monocultures in summer 2019, following the protocol from Garnier et al.
